title: The Directed Handshake Lemma and Tournament Score Sums
description: Supplies the degree-counting foundation underlying the directed Hamiltonicity theorems of Erdős #1012's oq-03 entry (Rédei, Moon–Moser, Ghouila–Houri, arc-count threshold), which all rely on degree sums that were never stated. Proves the directed handshake lemma — ∑ outDegree(v) = arcCount = ∑ inDegree(v) — so total out-degree equals total in-degree. For tournaments it pins the global statistics exactly: outDegree v + inDegree v = n − 1, 2·arcCount = n(n−1), and Landau's score-sum identity 2·∑ outDegree(v) = n(n−1); plus the averaging/pigeonhole step n·outDegree(v) ≥ arcCount for some v. Self-contained and fully machine-checked (the companion oq-03 file is itself axiomatized).

mathlibDependencies.description: Fintype.card {a // p a} = (univ.filter p).card — converts the noncomputable degree/arc-count definitions to Finset filter cardinalities
(s.filter p).card = ∑ a ∈ s, if p a then 1 else 0 — the bridge from filter cardinality to an indicator sum
∑ over a product Finset equals the iterated double sum — turns the arc-set sum into ∑ᵥ ∑ᵤ
(s ∪ t).card = s.card + t.card for disjoint s, t — used for the tournament out/in neighbourhood partition
A nonempty Finset attains a maximum of any function into a linear order — the pigeonhole witness for above-average out-degree

relatedProblems.relationship: Companion: 'Directed Graph Hamiltonian Cycle Thresholds' (Rédei, Moon–Moser, Ghouila–Houri, arc-count threshold). This entry supplies the degree-counting identities those proofs rest on, fully verified.
Root: Erdős Problem #1012 (Long Cycles in Dense Graphs).

overview.historicalContext: The handshake lemma — that the degree sum of a graph equals twice the number of edges — is the oldest result in graph theory, implicit in Euler's 1736 Königsberg paper. Its directed form splits into two halves (out-degrees and in-degrees), each recovering the arc count. For tournaments (orientations of complete graphs, studied by H. G. Landau in 1953 for animal-dominance ranking models), the degree sequence is the *score sequence*, and the elementary identity that scores sum to n(n−1)/2 is the entry point to Landau's theorem characterising score sequences.
overview.problemStatement: The companion entry erdos-1012-oq-03 (directed Hamiltonicity thresholds: Rédei, Moon–Moser, Ghouila–Houri, arc-count) rests on degree-sum identities that were never stated there. State and fully verify those foundations: the directed handshake lemma ∑ᵥ outDegree(v) = arcCount = ∑ᵥ inDegree(v), the tournament specialisations (outDegree v + inDegree v = n − 1, 2·arcCount = n(n−1), Landau's score-sum identity), and the averaging/pigeonhole step that opens degree-threshold arguments.
overview.proofStrategy: Both handshake identities are a single counting principle viewed two ways: the arc set {(u,v) : u → v} fibers over its first coordinate as ⨆ᵥ {u : v → u} (giving ∑ outDegree) and over its second as ⨆ᵥ {u : u → v} (giving ∑ inDegree). Formally each degree and the arc count are rewritten as Finset.filter cardinalities, then card_filter turns them into indicator sums and sum_product splits the arc-set sum over V × V; the in-degree form is the out-degree form plus a coordinate swap (Finset.sum_comm). For tournaments, the out- and in-neighbourhoods of v are disjoint and exhaust univ ∖ {v} (card_union_of_disjoint + card_erase), giving outDegree v + inDegree v = n − 1; summing over v with both handshake forms yields 2·arcCount = n(n−1) and Landau's identity. The averaging bound takes a vertex maximising out-degree and bounds the handshake sum termwise.
keyInsights: Both handshake identities are one counting principle seen twice: the arc set fibers over its source coordinate (∑ outDegree) and over its target coordinate (∑ inDegree), so the in-degree form is the out-degree form composed with Finset.sum_comm — and total out-degree therefore equals total in-degree.

Expressing the noncomputable subtype-cardinality degrees as Finset.filter cardinalities (card_filter → indicator sum) is what lets the abstract arc count be split by Finset.sum_product into the iterated double sum over vertices.

In a tournament the out- and in-neighbourhoods of each vertex partition univ ∖ {v}, so outDegree v + inDegree v = n − 1 vertex-by-vertex; summing collapses to the global 2·arcCount = n(n−1) and Landau's score-sum identity 2·∑ outDegree = n(n−1).

The averaging step n·outDegree(v) ≥ arcCount for some v — the maximum out-degree exceeds the average — is the elementary first move of every degree-threshold (Dirac/Ghouila–Houri-type) Hamiltonicity argument, and falls out of the handshake sum by a termwise bound.

These identities are used silently throughout tournament theory and the companion's Hamiltonicity proofs yet were never stated there; isolating and machine-checking them gives a reusable, 0-axiom degree-counting toolkit.

sections.title: Header: The Directed Handshake Lemma and Tournament Score Sums
sections.summary: Module docstring: notes the companion file's Hamiltonicity theorems rest on degree-counting identities that were never stated there, and states this file's headline result — the directed handshake lemma ∑outDegree = arcCount = ∑inDegree — together with its tournament specializations (outDegree+inDegree=n−1, 2·arcCount=n(n−1), the Landau score-sum identity) and a pigeonhole averaging consequence used by Ghouila–Houri-style threshold arguments.
sections.mathContext: Directed handshake lemma: $\sum_v \mathrm{outDegree}(v) = \mathrm{arcCount} = \sum_v \mathrm{inDegree}(v)$; for tournaments, $\mathrm{outDegree}(v)+\mathrm{inDegree}(v)=n-1$, $2\cdot\mathrm{arcCount}=n(n-1)$, and $2\sum_v\mathrm{outDegree}(v)=n(n-1)$ (Landau's identity).

sections.title: §0: Digraph definitions
sections.summary: Mirrors the companion file's loopless Digraph structure with noncomputable outDegree, inDegree, arcCount (as subtype cardinalities) and the IsTournament predicate, so the file is self-contained and verifiable end to end.
sections.mathContext: Degrees and arc count are cardinalities of subtypes of V and V × V; an `open scoped Classical` makes their decidability uniform with the filter reformulation.

sections.title: §1–2: Filter reformulation and the handshake lemma
sections.summary: Private lemmas express each degree and the arc count as Finset.filter cardinalities; then sum_outDegree_eq_arcCount and sum_inDegree_eq_arcCount prove ∑ outDegree = arcCount = ∑ inDegree via the product decomposition of the arc set, yielding sum_outDegree_eq_sum_inDegree.
sections.mathContext: Each filter card is rewritten to an indicator sum (Finset.card_filter); the arc-set sum over V × V is split with Finset.sum_product, and the in-degree form adds Finset.sum_comm.

sections.title: §3: Tournament score sums
sections.summary: tournament_outDegree_add_inDegree (out + in = n − 1, by partitioning univ ∖ {v} into out- and in-neighbours), then tournament_two_mul_arcCount (2·arcCount = n(n−1)) and Landau's tournament_two_mul_sum_outDegree.
sections.mathContext: In a tournament the out- and in-neighbourhoods of v are disjoint and exhaust the other n − 1 vertices; summing the per-vertex identity over all v and using both handshake forms gives 2·arcCount = n(n−1).

sections.title: §4: Averaging / pigeonhole
sections.summary: exists_outDegree_ge_average: some vertex has n·outDegree(v) ≥ arcCount — the maximum out-degree is at least the average, the first step of degree-threshold Hamiltonicity arguments.
sections.mathContext: Take a vertex maximising out-degree; bounding the handshake sum termwise by n copies of that maximum gives the inequality.

conclusion.summary: The directed handshake lemma (∑ outDegree = arcCount = ∑ inDegree, hence total out-degree = total in-degree) and its tournament specialisations (out + in = n − 1, 2·arcCount = n(n−1), Landau's score sum, and the averaging bound) furnish the degree-counting foundation that the companion's Hamiltonicity theorems use implicitly. Everything is proved from first principles, sorry-free and 0-axiom.
implications: Supplies the degree-counting foundation the companion Hamiltonicity theorems (Rédei, Moon–Moser, Ghouila–Houri, arc-count threshold) rest on but never state: the directed handshake lemma ∑ d⁺ = arcCount = ∑ d⁻ is the directed analogue of Euler's handshake lemma, and its tournament specialisations pin the global statistics exactly.

The Landau score-sum identity 2·∑ d⁺ = n(n−1) (scores sum to C(n,2)) and the averaging bound 'some vertex beats the average' are the elementary entry points to tournament degree-threshold arguments, now available sorry-free and 0-axiom for reuse.

Re-declaring the digraph definitions verbatim makes the file self-contained and end-to-end machine-checked, decoupling the counting layer from the (separately maintained) companion so the identities can be cited independently.
openQuestions: Build toward Landau's theorem: a non-decreasing sequence is the score sequence of a tournament iff its partial sums dominate the triangular numbers with equality at the end (the majorization characterisation of realisable score sequences).
Repair or replace the companion oq-03 file so its Hamiltonicity proofs cite these handshake and tournament-score lemmas directly instead of re-deriving the degree counting implicitly.

mainTheorems.name: sum_outDegree_eq_arcCount
mainTheorems.description: Directed handshake lemma: summing out-degrees over all vertices recovers the total arc count.

mainTheorems.name: sum_outDegree_eq_sum_inDegree
mainTheorems.description: Conservation of degree: total out-degree equals total in-degree.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∑ v : V, D.outDegree v = ∑ v : V, D.inDegree v

mainTheorems.name: tournament_outDegree_add_inDegree
mainTheorems.description: In a tournament each vertex beats or loses to every other, so its out- and in-degrees sum to n − 1.
mainTheorems.leanType: D.IsTournament → D.outDegree v + D.inDegree v = Fintype.card V - 1

mainTheorems.name: tournament_two_mul_arcCount
mainTheorems.description: A tournament on n vertices has exactly n(n−1)/2 arcs (stated as 2·arcCount = n(n−1) to stay in ℕ).

mainTheorems.name: tournament_two_mul_sum_outDegree
mainTheorems.description: Landau's identity: the score sequence of a tournament sums to n(n−1)/2.
mainTheorems.leanType: D.IsTournament → 2 * ∑ v : V, D.outDegree v = Fintype.card V * (Fintype.card V - 1)

mainTheorems.name: exists_outDegree_ge_average
mainTheorems.description: Pigeonhole: some vertex has out-degree at least the average.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∃ v : V, Fintype.card V * D.outDegree v ≥ D.arcCount
